chunks: Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah narrated from his father, from Yunus, from Abdillah ibn Sinan or Ibn Muskān, from Abū al-Jārūd, who said:
Abū Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: "When I narrate something to you, ask me about it in the Book of Allah, Exalted and Glorious."
Then he said in his narration: "Indeed, Allah, the Exalted, forbade al-qīl (rumor-mongering/saying and being said), al-qāl (idle talk), corruption of wealth, and frequent questioning."
They said: "O son of the Messenger of Allah, where is this in the Book of Allah, Exalted and Glorious?"

He said: "Indeed, Allah, Exalted and Glorious, says in His Book: 'There is no good in much of their private counsel, except for he who commands a charity or a good deed or reconciliation between people' (1)" — the verse.
And Allah, the Exalted, says: 'And do not give the foolish your wealth, which Allah has made a means of support for you' (2).
And He says: 'Do not ask about things which, if they are made clear to you, will cause you distress' (3).

key_terms.الْقِيلُ وَالْقَالُ: Idle talk and rumor-mongering; saying and being said

ai.seo_question: How does the Quran prohibit idle talk and excessive questioning according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Imam al-Bāqir (peace be upon him) establishes the Quran as the ultimate criterion for validating his teachings, specifically linking the prohibition of idle talk (al-qīl wa al-qāl) and wealth corruption to divine verses. This narration highlights the Shia scholarly principle that the Ahl al-Bayt’s interpretations are inextricably bound to the Quranic text, ensuring that legal and ethical rulings remain rooted in revelation. By explicitly connecting these concepts to verses on private counsel, wealth management, and avoiding trivial inquiries, the Imam demonstrates the coherence between prophetic tradition and the Quranic message.
